summary: Discusses and formalizes channel binding: tying authentication done at a higher layer to the secure channel set up at a lower layer, so both sides know they are the same endpoints. This lets applications rely on lower-layer protection while still getting the assurance they need. It also describes the pros, cons and security considerations.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a secret phone call. Channel binding is checking that the person you proved your identity to is the very same person on the line, not someone cutting in between.

subtitle: How to prove that an application-level login and the secure channel underneath it share the same two ends.

tldr.problem: Applications want to authenticate users themselves yet let a lower layer such as IPsec protect the session, but without a link between the two a man-in-the-middle could sit at the lower layer.
tldr.mechanism: Channel binding names the lower-layer channel (or its end-points) with data that both sides can compare at the higher layer, and the RFC sets requirements for doing this safely.
tldr.outcome: Applications can delegate session protection downward for performance while still ruling out a man-in-the-middle, with caveats about weaker ciphers and non-unique bindings.

today: RFC 5056 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text describes SASL support, IPsec channel bindings and several related drafts as work still in progress in November 2007.

sections.title: The Problem Channel Binding Solves
sections.content:
Sometimes an application wants to handle authentication itself while using session or transport security at a lower network layer. IPsec, for example, can be accelerated in hardware to handle very high link speeds, but its key exchange and architecture are not well suited to use as a security mechanism inside applications that have users as clients. Combining the layers is attractive, but they must be bound together to avoid man-in-the-middle (MITM) vulnerabilities.

The term comes from the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), whose channel binding facility was meant for binding authentication to lower-layer channels. This RFC generalizes and formalizes the idea independent of the GSS-API. It expects use with other frameworks such as SASL and even with protocols that have their own authentication, and also for analyzing security protocols.

The main goal is to delegate cryptographic session protection to layers below the application so hardware implementations can be used. The critical problem is ensuring there is no MITM, from the application's point of view, at the lower layer. As an example, iSCSI does application-layer authentication but relies on IPsec for transport protection and provides no binding between the two, so initiators must informally check that the authenticated server name matches the IPsec peer.
sections.plainLanguage: You show your ID to a guard at the front desk, but a stranger might be standing in the hallway pretending to be that guard. Channel binding checks that the hallway and the desk are the same person.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.content:
A secure channel is a packet, datagram, octet stream connection or sequence of connections between two end-points that gives cryptographic integrity and, optionally, confidentiality to the data. Channel binding (a noun) is the process of establishing that no MITM exists between two end-points that were authenticated at one layer but use a secure channel at a lower layer.

Channel bindings (plural) are data that name a channel or its end-points, so that if the data is shown at a higher layer to be the same at both ends, there is no MITM. There are two kinds. Unique channel bindings name a channel in a cryptographically secure manner and uniquely in time. End-point channel bindings name the authenticated end-points, or one end-point, of a channel and are securely bound to it, but do not identify the channel uniquely in time.

The RFC also defines cryptographic binding: an operation that makes an object such as a key or a secure channel "speak for" a principal. It admits that the one-letter difference between "binding" and "bindings" is confusing. EAP also uses the phrase "channel binding" for something that looks similar but is different, and EAP is out of scope here.
sections.plainLanguage: The channel is a tunnel. A channel binding is a name tag for the tunnel, and if both ends read out the same name tag, nobody swapped tunnels in the middle.

sections.title: Requirements for Channel Binding
sections.content:
Applications that use channel binding MUST verify that the same channel bindings are seen at both ends, and MUST use an application-layer authentication protocol to authenticate at least one peer. If that protocol supports channel binding the application SHOULD use it, and it MUST have an input slot for a handle to the channel or its bindings. If it does not, but offers at least integrity protection, the application MUST use that protection to exchange the bindings or hashes of them. The type of channel binding MUST be named, and for nested channels of the same type the innermost is used.

Specifications MUST give a single canonical octet string encoding, starting with the channel binding unique prefix followed by a colon. Bindings MUST be built so an MITM cannot easily force one channel's bindings to match another's. Unique bindings MUST cover the key exchange and any negotiation and authentication used to set up the channel. End-point bindings MUST be bound into the channel and all its negotiations, and applications SHOULD prefer cryptographic quantities such as certificate-subject public keys.

Revealing the bindings MUST NOT weaken the channel, failures MUST be reported to applications, and applications MUST NOT send sensitive data over the channel before the binding operation completes. If the channel lacks confidentiality, applications that want it MUST provide it at the application layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: compare the name tags, write them down in one agreed way, make them hard to fake, and do not whisper secrets until the check passes.

sections.title: GSS-API and SASL
sections.content:
The GSS-API supports channel binding when a security context is set up, though mechanisms are not required to support it. GSS-API mechanisms must fail context establishment when binding fails, and there is no negotiation of channel binding, so applications must agree in advance on whether to use it. The RFC notes that pseudo-mechanisms wrapping existing ones could allow negotiation inside protocols such as NFSv4 and SSHv2 that negotiate GSS-API mechanisms.

At the time of writing SASL did not yet provide channel binding, and work was ongoing to add it. The RFC expects SASL to differ in that a binding result would only affect negotiation of SASL security layers: when binding succeeds, SASL should select no security layer and leave session protection to the bound channel.

Where a framework offers no suitable facility, application protocols MAY include a separate protected exchange of channel bindings, which requires at least integrity protection from the authentication service.
sections.plainLanguage: Some login systems already have a built-in spot for the name tag check and others do not. When they do not, you can pass the name tag along inside a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Examples for SSH and TLS
sections.content:
Specifications of channel bindings for specific channels are kept elsewhere. The RFC lists SSHv2 and TLS as having them and says there is no specification yet for IPsec channel bindings, though the BTNS working group was working on IPsec channels. Its examples are explicitly not normative.

For SSHv2, the session ID suffices as a unique binding, since it cryptographically binds key exchange and negotiation. For TLS, the session ID does not work because the server simply assigns it, so an MITM posing as the server could give the victim the same ID. Instead the initial, unencrypted TLS finished messages can be used, since they come from the TLS pseudo-random function keyed with the session key over all handshake material.

As end-point bindings, the SSHv2 host public key and the TLS server certificate can work, but not all key exchanges or cipher suites involve them, which limits their usefulness.
sections.plainLanguage: For each kind of tunnel you need something that cannot be copied by a trickster. A number the server just hands out can be copied, but a fingerprint made from the whole secret setup cannot.

sections.title: Uses and Benefits
sections.content:
The identified uses are delegating session protection to layers where hardware can be expected to help, and reducing the number of live cryptographic contexts an application keeps. Examples given are NFSv4 and iSCSI delegating protection to ESP/AH, with RDDP or RDMA hardware offload, and HTTP with TLS where authentication at the HTTP layer is bound to a TLS channel between proxies.

RDDP offload cannot work when layers above it use privacy protection. Moving that protection down to IPsec, below RDDP, lets RDDP see application data in cleartext relative to its own headers. For NFSv4, which multiplexes many users onto one connection with a GSS-API context each, binding to IPsec would mean far fewer contexts per connection.

The listed benefits are avoiding double protection of data, using hardware-accelerated IPsec, integrating RDDP offload with IPsec acceleration, and lower latency for multiplexing applications. The RFC says that delegating to IPsec needs features not yet specified, such as IPsec channels, related APIs and IPsec channel bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking every single letter and then locking the whole mailbag is wasted work. If the mailbag lock is strong and you are sure it is the right bag, you can skip the extra locks and go faster.

sections.title: The Channel Bindings Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a registry of channel bindings specifications, both to keep names unique and to point to the technical specification for each. There is no naming convention: any string of US-ASCII alphanumerics, period and dash will do.

Registration needs expert review, with a request template sent to a public mailing list and IANA, and two weeks for community input. The template records the unique prefix, whether the binding is "unique" or "end-point", the channel type, whether the binding is secret, and the intended usage (COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE). Registrations may not be deleted, only marked OBSOLETE, and the IESG owns bindings on the IETF standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official phone book of name-tag types so every kind has its own unique name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Delegating protection from one layer to another almost certainly involves trade-offs, such as weaker cipher modes in one layer than the other. Comparing their strengths is difficult and out of scope, so implementors and administrators should understand them. Interfaces could offer a security profile notion so applications avoid channels too weak for their needs.

Channel binding makes anonymous channels, where neither end is strongly authenticated, useful, and implementors should avoid making it easy to use such channels without it. Overall security depends on the channel, how its bindings are constructed and the application-layer authentication. Revealing bindings must not weaken a channel, though end-point bindings may disclose the peers' identities.

Non-unique bindings used for fast re-authentication are risky on multi-user systems. In the NFSv4 over IPsec example, another user who connects directly to port 2049 and merely asserts RPCSEC_GSS handles would share the client's bindings and could impersonate any authenticated user. The server should require re-authentication and binding, or the channel should offer confidentiality and use hard-to-guess random cookies.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in a building shares one front door, a sneaky person can walk in behind someone and claim to be them. So each person has to show their ID again.
